The Tobii Pro Glasses 3 save each recording as a folder on the SD card. Inside are the [scene video]{.hl}, a [metadata file]{.hl} called `recording.g3` and three gzipped JSON files with one record per line: `gazedata.gz`, `imudata.gz` and `eventdata.gz`. glasses3 reads these files directly, without going through Tobii Pro Lab. The data come back as [tibbles]{.hl}, so this guide also loads dplyr to work with them.

```{r}
library(glasses3)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

## Reading a recording

`read_g3()` takes the path to a recording folder. The package includes the first 30 seconds of a recording, with the identifying metadata replaced by placeholders.

```{r}
rec <- read_g3(g3_example())
rec
```

The result is a list with the metadata and a tibble for each stream. The [gaze data]{.hl} have one row per sample. Samples where the glasses lost the eyes keep their row, with `NA` values.

```{r}
names(rec$gaze)
summary(rec)
```

The [`valid` column]{.hl} says whether a sample has a gaze point. The glasses can estimate gaze from one eye, so a sample can be valid while one of `valid_left` and `valid_right` is `FALSE`.

## Several recordings

`list_g3_recordings()` searches a folder, such as the root of an SD card, and lists every recording it finds with its name, participant, start time and duration. The readers `read_g3_gaze()`, `read_g3_imu()` and `read_g3_events()` accept this list, or a vector of paths, and stack the recordings into one tibble. The [`recording` column]{.hl} says which folder each row comes from.

```{r}
recordings <- list_g3_recordings(dirname(g3_example()))
recordings
gaze <- read_g3_gaze(recordings)
events <- read_g3_events(recordings)
```

The functions for sync port pulses and epochs below work on such data too. They match the samples of each recording to that recording's pulses, and the plots draw one panel per recording.

## Pupil diameter

The sync port connects the glasses to other equipment. A stimulus computer can send a pulse at each stimulus onset, which the glasses record with the [direction]{.hl} `"in"`. The glasses can also send pulses that another device records, with the direction `"out"`. The functions use `"in"` by default. The example recording only holds pulses sent by the glasses, so the examples here use `direction = "out"`.

```{r}
plot_g3_pupil(rec, direction = "out")
```

The grey areas mark the [sync port pulses]{.hl}. `g3_syncport()` lists them with their onsets and offsets.

```{r}
g3_syncport(rec$events, direction = "out")
```

`g3_add_syncport()` keeps every sample and adds the sync port state, the number of the most recent pulse and the time since its onset. This suits models of the whole recording, where cutting epochs would drop the samples between pulses.

```{r}
tagged <- g3_add_syncport(rec$gaze, rec$events, direction = "out")
tagged |>
  filter(syncport == 1) |>
  select(time, pulse, pulse_time)
```

Long recordings are hard to read at 50 samples per second. The `smooth` argument draws a [running median]{.hl} over the raw trace, here one second wide. Short blinks do not pull it down, and the data themselves are not changed.

```{r}
plot_g3_pupil(rec, direction = "out", smooth = 1)
```

## Epochs

`g3_epochs()` cuts the samples into [epochs]{.hl} around each pulse onset. It numbers the epochs in the `epoch` column and adds the time relative to the onset. After `g3_pupil_long()`, there is one row per sample and eye, which suits ggplot2 and mixed-effects models.

```{r}
ep <- g3_epochs(rec$gaze, rec$events, before = 0.5, after = 5, direction = "out")
pupil <- g3_pupil_long(ep)
head(pupil)
```

The onsets do not have to be sync port pulses. `g3_epochs()` also takes a data frame with an `onset` column, such as the [trial onsets]{.hl} of an experiment, and copies its other columns to the samples of each epoch.

```{r}
trials <- data.frame(onset = c(2, 12, 22), condition = c("a", "b", "a"))
trial_epochs <- g3_epochs(rec$gaze, trials, before = 0.5, after = 3)
count(trial_epochs, epoch, condition)
```

An experiment script can also send events to the glasses through their API, each with a tag and an object. `g3_api_events()` extracts these [API events]{.hl} from the event data, and its output can be passed to `g3_epochs()` in the same way. The example recording has none.

Given epochs, `plot_g3_pupil()` puts the time from the onset on the x axis. Each eye gets its own panel, with a thin line per epoch and the mean drawn on top.

```{r}
plot_g3_pupil(ep)
```

Before analysis, `g3_quality()` shows how much data each epoch holds: the number of samples, the proportion with a gaze point and with data for each eye, and the [longest gap]{.hl} without a gaze point. Epochs with too much missing data can then be dropped.

```{r}
quality <- g3_quality(ep)
quality
```

For models of the whole time course, such as generalised additive mixed models, `g3_downsample()` averages the samples into [time bins]{.hl}. Bins are counted from the onset, and a bin where more than half of the samples are missing is left empty. Character columns, such as a participant or condition label, are dropped unless you name them in `by`, and the groups of a grouped tibble are kept.

```{r}
binned <- g3_downsample(pupil, bin = 0.1)
head(binned)
```

glasses3 leaves [pupil preprocessing]{.hl} to other packages. PupillometryR, gazer and eyeris handle blink removal, interpolation and baseline correction.

## Gaze position

`plot_g3_gaze()` shows where the wearer looked in the scene camera image. The top of the plot is the top of the video frame.

```{r, fig.height = 4}
plot_g3_gaze(rec)
```

`g3_gaze_angles()` turns the gaze direction of each eye into [azimuth]{.hl} and [elevation]{.hl} in degrees, relative to straight ahead of the glasses, and adds the [vergence]{.hl} angle between the eyes.

```{r}
angles <- g3_gaze_angles(rec$gaze)
angles |>
  select(left_azimuth, left_elevation, vergence) |>
  summary()
```

`g3_gaze_velocity()` adds the [angular velocity]{.hl} of each eye from one sample to the next, in degrees per second. It is not smoothed, and can be the starting point for detecting fixations and saccades.

```{r}
velocity <- g3_gaze_velocity(rec$gaze)
velocity |>
  select(left_velocity, right_velocity) |>
  summary()
```

## Clock time

`g3_add_clock_time()` adds the date and time of each sample, from the start time stored in the recording. The [clock time]{.hl} helps to align the data with other devices that log the time of day.

```{r}
g3_add_clock_time(rec$gaze, rec) |>
  select(time, clock_time) |>
  head()
```

## Scene video

The scene camera films at 25 frames per second. `g3_add_frame()` adds the number of the [video frame]{.hl} shown at each sample, counted from 0, so that codes made frame by frame from the video, such as areas of interest, can be joined to the samples. The first frame is taken to start with the recording. If an event visible in the video shows otherwise, set `start` to the time of the first frame.

```{r}
g3_add_frame(rec$gaze) |>
  select(time, frame, gaze2d_x, gaze2d_y) |>
  head()
```

## Damaged files and gaps

A file that was cut off, for example by an interrupted copy from the SD card, is still read. The readers skip the damaged lines, return the intact samples and give a warning that names the skipped lines. A file whose compressed data are damaged cannot be read and gives an error. `g3_fill_gaps()` then inserts empty rows where samples are missing, so the time series is evenly spaced again before preprocessing.

```{r}
filled <- g3_fill_gaps(rec$gaze)
count(filled, inserted)
```

## IMU data

The glasses sample the accelerometer and gyroscope together, while the magnetometer runs separately at a lower rate. Each row of the [IMU data]{.hl} therefore has missing values for the sensors that were not sampled at that moment.

```{r}
head(rec$imu)
```
